case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Motor Components (KMC) is a public limited company in the automotive components sector, employing a workforce of 95. Founded in 1998 by Nadia Kestrel, it grinds precision gears for vehicle assemblers from two plants and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. KMC plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated gear-grinding line, financed by a $700,000 bank loan and a five-year lease on the grinding machines. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $21 a unit and a selling price of $35, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. KMC faces two problems: a defect rate of 2.8% on gears and labour turnover of 11%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality Report — Q3 2025: The plants ground 17,500 gears last quarter at a defect rate of 2.8%, down from 3.9% a year earlier. Warranty claims fell from 52 to 31 a month and average delivery time is 3.8 days. A survey of 650 vehicle assemblers found 61% would switch supplier for a two-day shorter lead time and 49% audit quality systems before placing orders. Some 30 of the 95 technicians need gear-grinding training; a certified course costs $1,400 per technician.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Motor Components as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing costs for firms with variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.49 an hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Alloy-steel input costs have risen 6.6% year-on-year, producer price inflation is 4.8%, and demand for vehicle components grew 4.2% over the same period.

questions.question_text: KMC plans to finance its $1,200,000 grinding line with a $700,000 bank loan and a five-year lease. Explain two advantages for KMC of the lease instead of borrowing to buy the machines.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A lease spreads the cost of the grinding machines over five years, so KMC does not pay $1,200,000 up front and the $700,000 bank loan can remain available for other working capital. With fixed costs of $420,000 a year and a 2.8% defect rate, preserving cash helps the firm cover the $1,400 per technician training for the 30 staff who need it while the line reaches 70,000 units.

Point 2: Under a lease the lessor usually maintains and replaces the machines, reducing the risk that a breakdown stops precision gear grinding and cuts the $14 contribution per unit. That suits a public limited company answerable to shareholders, because the $1,200,000 investment need not appear as a large immediate debt; the trade-off is that total lease payments can exceed a purchase price and the asset is never owned, but cash flow is protected during the 11% turnover problem. It also avoids tying up security against the two plants.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KMC's investment, costs and cash flow.

questions.question_text: KMC is promoting faster delivery of precision gears. Consider sponsoring a motorsport team, hosting technical webinars, or direct mail to vehicle assemblers. Which should KMC choose to win assemblers? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Sponsoring a motorsport team: Motor racing gives KMC high brand visibility and links its gears to performance engineering, which can impress the 650 assemblers surveyed. It is glamorous and memorable. However, sponsorship fees are large for a firm funding a $1,200,000 line with a $700,000 loan, and the link to a 3.8-day delivery promise is weak; most viewers are not purchasing engineers, so the spend is largely untargeted.

Technical webinars: Online webinars let KMC demonstrate grinding accuracy, explain the fall in defects from 3.9% to 2.8% and answer engineers' questions live, directly addressing the 49% who audit quality systems. They are low-cost, measurable and can be replayed, and delivery improvements can be explained to many assemblers at once. The weakness is that attendance must be earned and webinars do not by themselves prove the two-day lead time the 61% want.

Direct mail to vehicle assemblers: Printed technical brochures mailed to named purchasing managers are highly targeted and can include certification data and delivery guarantees. They suit a small, identifiable customer set. Drawbacks are printing and postage costs, low response rates, and no immediate feedback, so a $1,200,000 investment cannot be justified on mail alone.

Recommendation: KMC should choose technical webinars as the lead channel, followed up by targeted direct mail to assemblers who attend. Webinars prove technical quality to the 49% who audit quality systems at low cost, and technical proof matters more than brand glamour. Motorsport sponsorship is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and direct mail alone is rejected as a weak one-way medium; combining it with webinars uses it where interest is already shown.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to KMC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KMC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of KMC with a justified recommendation explaining why sponsorship and mail-only are rejected.

questions.question_text: KMC has a 2.8% defect rate and 11% labour turnover. Explain two benefits for KMC of using democratic leadership with its technicians.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 95 technicians to suggest improvements, and those closest to the grinders are best placed to explain the 2.8% defect rate. Consulting them fits a hierarchical structure that still values participation, and practical ideas can cut warranty claims from 52 to 31 a month, protecting the $14 contribution on each of the 17,500 gears made last quarter.

Point 2: Being consulted raises job satisfaction and can ease the 11% turnover, which is costly when 30 technicians still need the $1,400 certified course. Technicians who help set quality targets are more likely to stay and to apply what they learn, supporting the 3.8-day delivery promise to the 650 assemblers surveyed. The cost is slower decisions, but for a public limited company facing skill shortages the commitment gain matters more. Consultation also builds acceptance of the changes needed to cut 11% turnover, so technicians stay long enough to apply the $1,400 course on the $1,200,000 line.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KMC's defects, turnover and training.

questions.question_text: KMC wants to reduce 11% labour turnover among its technicians. Consider an individual production bonus or company-wide profit sharing. Which should KMC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Individual production bonus: Paying a bonus tied to output and the 2.8% defect rate rewards each technician directly and can raise effort and precision on the $1,200,000 grinding line. It is easy to link to the 17,500 gears made last quarter and can be varied with results, so cost rises only when output rises. The drawback is that individual bonuses can discourage teamwork and encourage speed over quality, and with 30 staff needing training, poorly set targets could raise defects and warranty claims.

Company-wide profit sharing: Sharing profit across the workforce of 95 encourages cooperation, which suits democratic leadership and the two-plant operation, and gives everyone a stake in the firm's performance. It can reduce turnover because staff feel rewarded when KMC succeeds. However, the link between an individual's work and the reward is weak, so free-riding is possible, and profits may be thin while the $700,000 loan and the lease are being serviced, meaning the payment could be small.

Decision: KMC should choose an individual production bonus with a quality condition attached, paying extra only when gears meet the 2.8% defect standard. It targets the effort that reduces defects and turnover directly and is affordable because it varies with output. Profit sharing is rejected because its reward is too remote from each technician's work and profits may be absorbed by financing costs; profit sharing can be introduced later once the line is profitable. The bonus can be tied to the 2.8% defect rate as well as output, so speed does not undermine the quality the 49% of assemblers audit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivators with limited application to KMC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both motivators in the context of KMC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivators in the context of KMC with a justified decision covering effort, teamwork and cost.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KMC's management can use its cost and break-even data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($35 − $21) = $420,000 ÷ $14 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $35 − $21 = $14. Answer: contribution per unit is $14.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KMC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 30,000 units against output of 70,000 units leaves a margin of safety of 40,000 units, showing the scale of demand loss the $1,200,000 grinding line can absorb before breaking even.
2. Contribution of $14 a gear lets managers evaluate the 61% of assemblers who would switch for a two-day shorter lead time: the extra volume from faster delivery can be valued in contribution before deciding how to organise the line.
3. The $700,000 bank loan and five-year lease can be tested against 30,000-unit break-even; above it each gear adds $14, so managers can check the line covers financing commitments.
4. Unit cost ($420,000 ÷ 70,000 units + $21 = $27 a gear) benchmarks the 17,500 gears ground last quarter and helps put a cost on the 2.8% defect rate and warranty claims, guiding the $1,400 training spend.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $14 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 40,000 units; valuing faster delivery for the 61% of assemblers; testing $700,000 loan and lease servicing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $27 to price the 2.8% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KMC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KMC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.57 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.97 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.13 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 inventories + $220,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $470,000; 2025 current assets = $200,000 + $250,000 + $90,000 = $540,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $300,000 in both years gives 1.57 and 1.80. Excluding inventories: ($470,000 − $180,000) ÷ $300,000 = $290,000 ÷ $300,000 = 0.97 in 2024, and ($540,000 − $200,000) ÷ $300,000 = $340,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.13 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The current ratio rose from 1.57 to 1.80 as current assets increased by $70,000 while current liabilities stayed at $300,000. The stricter measure rose from 0.97 to 1.13, so by 2025 KMC can meet short-term debts without selling gear inventories — useful while it pays a five-year lease and services a $700,000 loan on a $1,200,000 line. Cash increased from $70,000 to $90,000, giving a larger immediate buffer for the $700,000 loan. A caution is that trade receivables grew from $220,000 to $250,000, tying up cash, and the 49% of assemblers who audit quality systems may delay payment if defects occur; inventories also rose to $200,000, so slow-moving stock needs control.

Conclusion: KMC's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher, and the stricter test now clears 1, so the gain does not depend on stock. The remaining weakness is rising receivables, so tighter credit control and defect reduction should be priorities before further borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KMC of using quality assurance circles to cut its 2.8% defect rate.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Quality circles let technicians discuss grinding problems together, which suits democratic leadership and can attack the rise in defects from 3.9% to 2.8% at source rather than inspecting after the event. Better prevention reduces warranty claims of 31 a month, protects the $14 contribution on 17,500 gears and helps satisfy the 49% of assemblers who audit quality systems.

Disadvantage: Circles take meeting time from production and need training to be effective, yet 30 of 95 technicians still require the $1,400 certified course. With a $700,000 loan and a lease to service, time spent in discussion may delay the 3.8-day delivery that 61% of assemblers value, and a quality circle cannot fix machine faults on the $1,200,000 line on its own. Circles cannot replace the $1,400 certified training the 30 technicians need, and with a $700,000 loan and a lease to service, management will want evidence that prevention reduces the cost of 31 warranty claims a month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KMC's defects, audit requirements and training needs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 6.6% rise in alloy-steel input costs will affect KMC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The rise is 4.75% − 4.00% = 0.75 percentage points. On the $700,000 variable-rate bank loan, extra interest = 0.75% × $700,000 = 0.0075 × $700,000 = $5,250 a year. This is modest against fixed costs of $420,000, and it is zero if the loan is fixed. The five-year lease is unaffected, so only a part of the $1,200,000 financing is exposed; the rate rise can largely be managed.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, $12.60 to $13.49 an hour): KMC employs a workforce of 95 and makes 70,000 gears, so labour productivity = 70,000 ÷ 95 = 736.8 gears per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be calculated honestly. The increase is compulsory and will lift unit labour costs unless productivity holds at that level; otherwise the $14 contribution per gear narrows, but the size cannot be stated from the data supplied.

Alloy-steel input-cost inflation (6.6%): The insert does not decompose the $21 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is shown: if the entire $21 rose 6.6%, the increase = 6.6% × $21 = 0.066 × $21 = $1.386 a gear; at 70,000 units a year that is 70,000 × $1.386 = $97,020. Even a fraction of that pass-through reduces contribution on every gear, and price increases may be hard to win when 61% of assemblers already threaten to switch for better delivery.

Conclusion: The 6.6% rise in alloy-steel input costs will have the greatest impact. It directly attacks the $14 contribution on 70,000 gears, with a computable upper-bound exposure of $97,020 a year, far larger than the $5,250 interest figure, and it cannot be offset by fixing a loan rate. The wage effect is real but unquantifiable from the insert. KMC should renegotiate steel contracts and use the $1,200,000 line's quality gains to justify prices before worrying about the smaller rate rise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KMC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on KMC's costs, revenue or financing with figures derived from the insert.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with shown derivations and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
